platforms.title: High Triglycerides Aren't Just About Fatty Food
platforms.meta_description: Cutting back on fried food but your triglycerides won't budge? Triglycerides respond much more to sugar, alcohol, and inactivity than to dietary fat itself.
platforms.body_html:
It's a common, confusing pattern on a lab report: cholesterol comes back normal, but triglycerides are still high, even after cutting back on fried and fatty foods. That's not a fluke — it's because triglycerides are a different kind of fat with a different source. They're made mostly in the liver out of leftover energy — extra glucose and alcohol the body doesn't burn right away — and packaged for storage or circulation. That means how much fat you eat matters less for this specific number than how much sugar, refined starch, and alcohol you're taking in, and how active you are.

Why Triglycerides Stay High When Fat Intake Goes Down

Because triglyceride synthesis happens mainly in the liver from surplus carbohydrate and alcohol, cutting dietary fat alone often leaves this number untouched. Research reviewed by nutrition and cardiology bodies has found that higher intake of added sugars is associated with higher triglyceride levels, distinct from total fat intake — the American Heart Association recommends keeping added sugar under 25 grams (about 6 teaspoons) a day for women and 36 grams (about 9 teaspoons) for men, specifically because sugar is one of the few dietary factors clearly tied to triglyceride levels. Alcohol adds to this directly: the liver processes alcohol before almost anything else, and that processing pushes it to make more triglycerides as a byproduct, which is why even moderate regular drinking can keep levels elevated no matter how "clean" the rest of the diet looks.

What Happens When You Fix This

Move more, specifically with aerobic activity. In one clinical study of patients with high triglycerides, a program of aerobic endurance training lowered triglycerides by about 25% and VLDL-triglycerides — the particles that carry them through the blood — by about 27%, without necessarily requiring major weight loss first; the effect came from the training itself. Cut back on refined carbohydrates and added sugar specifically, not fat across the board — white bread, pastries, sugary drinks, and candy do more to this number than olive oil or nuts do. And take a hard look at alcohol intake, since even a few drinks a week can be enough to keep triglycerides elevated in people who are sensitive to it; a temporary break is often the fastest way to see whether alcohol was the hidden driver. None of this requires giving up fat entirely — the point is that the wrong target was being cut all along.

So the next time triglycerides come back high, is fried food really what changed — or was it the soda, the wine, or the couch? It's worth knowing your actual number too: a fasting triglyceride level under 150 mg/dL is generally considered normal, 150 to 199 borderline-high, and 200 or above high, with levels above 500 carrying a separate risk of pancreatitis that needs prompt medical attention rather than lifestyle changes alone. If your triglycerides stay high despite cutting sugar, alcohol, and adding regular activity, it's worth asking a doctor about underlying causes like poorly controlled blood sugar or thyroid function, since those can drive the number up independently of diet.
